> **Key takeaways**
> - A waiver and clear written policies tell parents what to expect before their child walks in.
> - Most waivers share the same core sections. Plain words make each one easier to sign.
> - Collect it before the first session, store it where you can find it, and review it every year.

**This is general information, not legal advice. Have a California lawyer review your waiver.** This guide covers what small studios and coaches commonly put in a waiver and how to run the paperwork smoothly. It does not tell you what the law requires or how a court would treat your form. Only a lawyer can do that for your business.

## Why a waiver and clear policies matter

The waiver is often the first document a parent reads from you. A clear, well-organised form tells them you have thought about their child's day.

It also starts a useful conversation. When a parent reads that your class involves climbing or contact drills, they can ask questions before the first session instead of during it.

Clear written policies do the same for everything around the class: who can pick a child up, what happens if a child feels unwell, how allergy information reaches staff, and whether a grown-up stays in the room. Written down once, your staff give the same answer every time.

## Common sections in a waiver for kids' activities

Your lawyer will shape the final wording, but many waivers for kids' classes share the same handful of sections.

### Participant and guardian information

The child's full name and date of birth, plus the parent or guardian's name, phone number and email. Many forms also list who else may pick the child up.

### A description of the activity and its risks

Describe what children actually do in your class, in the same plain words you use on your listing. "Kids practise forward rolls and cartwheels on padded mats" is clearer than a general phrase about physical activity. Then describe the risks a parent should know about, in the context of your real class: falls, bumps, minor strains, equipment use, outdoor heat. The aim is for a parent to understand what they are agreeing to.

### Medical information, emergency contact and consent

Space for allergies, conditions and medications a parent wants you to know about, plus one or two emergency contacts. Many forms also ask the parent to consent to first aid and to emergency care if they cannot be reached. Ask only for what your staff need to keep the child safe, and decide in advance who on your team can see it.

### Photo and media consent, as a separate opt-in

If you share class photos online, make this its own clearly marked choice, with a separate box or signature, rather than tucking it into the main waiver. A parent happy to sign for the activity may still want their child kept offline, and staff should be able to check that choice quickly.

### Signature and date

The parent or guardian's signature, printed name and the date. If your form is digital, make sure the record shows who signed and when.

## Keep it readable for parents

A parent often signs a waiver on a phone, standing in a lobby, with a child pulling at their sleeve. Write for that moment:

- **Use short sentences and plain words.** If a sentence needs a second read, split it.
- **Use headings** that match the sections above, so a parent can find the part they care about.
- **Put the important choices where they can be seen.** Photo consent and pick-up permissions should never be hidden in a long paragraph.
- **Match your listing.** The activity described in the waiver should be the one described on your class page. If you need help writing that page, see [how to write a kids' class listing parents actually book](/blog/how-to-write-a-kids-class-listing-parents-book).
- **Keep one version per activity type** if your classes differ a lot.

## Collect it before the first session

The worst time to hand a parent a form is two minutes before class. Rushed forms come back half filled in.

Make the waiver part of signing up, not part of arriving:

1. **Send it with the booking confirmation**, or have it signed as part of booking.
2. **Remind families before the first session** that it needs to be done.
3. **Have a plan for the family who arrives without it.** A tablet at the front desk or a few printed copies saves the moment, but decide in advance what your staff do.
4. **Check the roster against signed forms** before the class begins, so nobody slips through.

## Store records safely

A signed waiver holds a child's name, a birth date and often medical notes, so treat it with care:

- **Paper forms:** keep them in a locked cabinet, filed by family or by class term.
- **Digital forms:** keep them in one account with a strong password, and limit who on your team can open them.
- **Make them easy to find.** If a question comes up months later, you should be able to pull the right form quickly.
- **Ask your lawyer how long to keep them** and how to dispose of old ones.

## Review it every year

Classes change: a new age group, a new space, new equipment. Once a year, and whenever your activities change, reread your waiver and policies:

- Does the activity description still match what children do?
- Are the risks listed still the right ones?
- Do the contact details and pick-up rules still work for your team?
- Is the photo opt-in still clear?

Then take the updated version back to your lawyer before you start using it. Note the date of each version, so you know which form each family signed.

## How ORYN Quest fits

On ORYN Quest, before a listing goes live, the vendor must choose one of three answers to the waiver question. Families sign in the app before booking, sign on paper at the first session, or there is no waiver.

"In the app" needs at least one required waiver switched on, and a family can't finish booking until they sign. In-app waiver records do include the signer's name and email. "On paper": the vendor collects and keeps it, and ORYN does not check it. With every answer, parents still accept ORYN's own Parent Waiver & Release before booking.

ORYN does not review what a vendor's waiver says, so the wording is yours, and your lawyer's review still matters. If you already use a paper waiver, an AI tool can turn a photo or PDF of it into editable text. The upload is deleted as soon as it has been read, and you check the text before saving.

## FAQ

### Is this legal advice?
No. This is general information, not legal advice. Have a California lawyer review your waiver.

### What does a waiver for kids' activities usually include?
Most cover participant and guardian information, a plain description of the activity and its risks, medical information with emergency contacts and consent for care, a separate photo and media opt-in, and a signature with the date.

### When should parents sign the waiver?
Before the first session, ideally as part of booking or right after it. Forms filled in at the door tend to be rushed and incomplete.

### Should photo consent be part of the main waiver?
Many studios make it a separate, clearly marked opt-in. That way a parent can agree to the activity while choosing whether their child appears in your photos, and your staff can check that choice quickly.

### How often should I update my waiver?
Review it once a year and whenever your activities, space or equipment change. Have your lawyer review each new version, and keep a note of which version each family signed.
